title: Write a recursive function for Fibonacci number (base: `fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1`, recursive: `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)`).
shortTitle: Write a Recursive Function for Fibonacci Number
keyPoints: Fibonacci has two base cases: fib(0) = 0 and fib(1) = 1, and fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
Naive recursion is O(2^n) because it recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times
Memoization caches each result on first computation, collapsing exponential work to O(n) time and O(n) space
Bottom-up iteration with two rolling variables gives O(n) time and O(1) space
Fibonacci numbers overflow a long around the 93rd term, so production code uses BigInteger
This problem is the classic introduction to overlapping subproblems and dynamic programming

s1_definition.oneliner: Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the previous two, starting from zero and one.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fibonacci sequence** – a series where each number equals the sum of the two preceding numbers, starting with zero and one.
- **Base cases** – `fib(0) = 0` and `fib(1) = 1` because the recursive case needs two previous values.
- **Recursive case** – `fib(n) = fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)` makes two recursive calls and sums the results.
- **Naive complexity** – the call tree branches twice at every level, giving O(2^n) time.
- **Memoization fix** – caching each result on first computation reduces time to O(n).
- **Rolling variables** – keeping only the last two values gives O(n) time with O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India runs a loyalty bonus scheme for recurring deposits. Month zero has a bonus of zero rupees, month one has a bonus of one rupee, and every month after that the bonus equals the sum of the previous two months. To know month twelve's bonus you need month eleven and month ten, and to know those you keep going back until you reach the two known starting months. Recomputing from scratch every time is wasteful, so the bank writes each bonus in a ledger once and reads it back whenever it is needed.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Naive Recursion Call Tree for fib(5)
  ────────────────────────────────────

                    fib(5)
                   /      \
              fib(4)       fib(3)
             /     \       /     \
         fib(3)  fib(2) fib(2) fib(1)
         /   \    / \    / \
     fib(2) fib(1) ...  ...  ...
      / \
  fib(1) fib(0)

  Same subproblems computed many times:
  fib(3) → computed 2 times
  fib(2) → computed 3 times
  fib(1) → computed 5 times
  fib(0) → computed 3 times
```

```text
  Bottom-Up Rolling Variables
  ───────────────────────────

  Step 0:  prev2 = 0    prev1 = 1
  Step 2:  prev2 = 1    prev1 = 1    (0 + 1)
  Step 3:  prev2 = 1    prev1 = 2    (1 + 1)
  Step 4:  prev2 = 2    prev1 = 3    (1 + 2)
  Step 5:  prev2 = 3    prev1 = 5    (2 + 3)

  Only two variables needed at any time → O(1) space
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Fibonacci sequence is a series where every number is the sum of the two before it, starting from zero and one. It has two base cases because the recursive case needs two previous values to add together. The naive recursive version is beautifully simple but exponentially slow, because it recomputes the same subproblems again and again. This is the exact condition that dynamic programming was invented to solve.

The first fix is memoization: keep the natural recursion but add a cache that stores each result on first computation and returns the stored value on repeat calls. This collapses the exponential call tree into O(n) distinct computations. The second fix is bottom-up iteration with two rolling variables, which avoids the recursion stack entirely and uses only O(1) space.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this pattern for a loyalty bonus scheme where each month's bonus equalled the sum of the previous two months. A customer could ask for the projection at any month, and with naive recursion a far-off month would freeze the screen. With the rolling bottom-up approach, the projection returned instantly even for large months. The senior-level addition is that Fibonacci numbers overflow a long around the 93rd term, so BigInteger is necessary for exact results.

Remember one sentence: Fibonacci is the classic example of overlapping subproblems, and the fix is to compute each value once using memoization or bottom-up rolling variables.
